title: SpaceX Barred China at the June 2026 IPO. The Kahlon Ledger, Unsealed This Month by the Delaware Supreme Court, Shows SpaceX Took at Least a Dozen Checks from China-, Hong Kong-, and Russia-Addressed Investors Between 2018 and 2021, Routed Through Tomales Bay Capital. SpaceX Has Not Denied the Ledger. CFIUS, ITAR, and Pentagon Contract-Eligibility Standards All Weight Foreign Ownership.
beat: SpaceX Tomales Bay Capital / Kahlon ledger — ProPublica Delaware Supreme Court unsealing reveals China/Russia–addressed investors 2018–2021 vs June 2026 IPO exclusion — June 26 2026
narrative: On Thursday 26 June 2026, ProPublica published an investigation revealing that SpaceX — which has publicly stated it would block investors from mainland China and Hong Kong from participating in its June 2026 IPO — had already allowed foreign money linked to those same regions to enter its cap table years earlier, routed through offshore hubs and a fund middleman called Tomales Bay Capital. The story is sourced from a sealed corporate-investor ledger, the 'Kahlon ledger,' that was unsealed this month by the Delaware Supreme Court in favor of ProPublica in a corporate dispute. The Kahlon ledger shows at least a dozen investors with addresses in mainland China, Hong Kong, or Russia who acquired SpaceX stakes between 2018 and 2021, in checks ranging from $800,000 to $40 million. The buying ran through Tomales Bay Capital, a firm run by Iqbaljit Kahlon, a longtime SpaceX insider whose own CFO testified that Kahlon had been around the company longer than he had. Tomales Bay Capital bought SpaceX stock directly, packaged it into investment funds, and sold slices to outside investors for a fee. One named check came from an entity tied to David Su, co-founder of the Beijing venture firm MPCi, which put in $15 million in 2020. There is no evidence Su acted improperly, and MPCi says he received no nonpublic information about SpaceX. ProPublica reported last year that SpaceX's standard approach was to let Chinese money in as long as it was routed through the Cayman Islands or other offshore secrecy hubs — the middleman structure handled the rest. The timing of the disclosure is structural. SpaceX went public in June 2026, and its S-1 filings and post-IPO public statements explicitly bar mainland-Chinese and Hong Kong investors from buying the IPO. The Kahlon ledger shows that investors with mainland-China, Hong-Kong, or Russia addresses held stakes acquired 5–8 years before the IPO. An outside investor in a Tomales Bay fund does not show up on SpaceX's own cap table as a Chinese national. The compliance exposure is concrete, not rhetorical. SpaceX sits inside CFIUS review, ITAR export rules, and Pentagon contract-eligibility standards that all weigh foreign ownership. A cap table seeded with China- and Russia-linked money, even in legal amounts routed through offshore structures, becomes a compliance liability that can resurface in contract renewals and clearance reviews.
analysis: 1. The Kahlon ledger is a real document, unsealed by court order — the highest evidentiary tier available without an SEC investigation. ProPublica obtained the investor list from a Delaware corporate dispute. The records stayed sealed until this month (June 2026), when the Delaware Supreme Court ruled in ProPublica's favor and ordered them public. The unsealing-by-court-order provenance is the load-bearing evidentiary fact: this is not a leak, not an anonymous-source allegation, not a self-published whistleblower document. The Delaware Supreme Court ruled on the public-interest balancing and ordered release. 2. At least a dozen China / Hong Kong / Russia–addressed investors, 2018–2021. The checks range from $800,000 to $40 million. The names are in the ledger. ProPublica reports them. SpaceX has not denied the ledger's contents. The numerical range matters: $800K is a small individual investor; $40M is a fund-of-funds or family-office scale. The 2018–2021 window covers the period when SpaceX was winning its first major Pentagon launch contracts (Falcon 9 STP-2 mission in June 2019, NRO launch contracts, GPS-III launches) and Starshield was being set up as a dedicated defense product. 3. Tomales Bay Capital as the routing middleman. Tomales Bay Capital (run by Iqbaljit Kahlon, a longtime SpaceX insider whose tenure predates his own CFO's) bought SpaceX stock directly, packaged it into investment funds, and sold fund interests to outside investors for a fee. This is a documented intermediary structure — not a shell company allegation, but a fund vehicle that SpaceX insiders used to manage third-party capital exposure. The 'longer than me' CFO testimony is the structural indicator: Kahlon's tenure predates the CFO's, which means the routing structure predates the post-2017 finance-compliance infrastructure that SpaceX would later need to pass IPO-grade due diligence. 4. The David Su / MPCi — $15 million 2020 check. MPCi's co-founder David Su's entity put $15 million into SpaceX via this structure in 2020. MPCi says Su received no nonpublic information. There is no allegation that Su acted improperly. The point is the structural one: a Beijing-based venture firm was indirectly exposed to SpaceX during the period when SpaceX was winning its first major Pentagon launch contracts, and the exposure was specifically engineered to be invisible on SpaceX's own cap table. The MPCi investment is the named anchor for the broader pattern. 5. The S-1 / IPO exclusion language. SpaceX's June 2026 IPO prospectus and post-IPO public statements explicitly exclude investors from mainland China and Hong Kong. This is the public-policy posture — and it is the posture SpaceX took to satisfy the Pentagon contract-renewal review and the CFIUS public-defense-contractor process. The Kahlon ledger shows the historical exposure that the public-policy posture does not address. The discrepancy between posture and history is the load-bearing finding. 6. The compliance exposure ladder. SpaceX is a public defense contractor — Falcon 9 launches national-security payloads (NRO, GPS-III, STP), Starshield is a dedicated defense product (announced 2022, with explicit national-security-saturation role), Starship has DOD contracts (the Vandyck / Vandenberg / Cape Canaveral infrastructure upgrades for national-security launch). CFIUS review, ITAR export-control rules, and Pentagon contract-eligibility standards (the same standards that have tripped other defense-adjacent firms with inadvertent foreign exposure — Kaspersky, ByteDance, Huawei, DJI) all weight foreign ownership. The Tomales Bay routing does not exempt SpaceX from those reviews — it just makes the review trail harder to follow. The 'harder to follow' is now moot: the Delaware Supreme Court ordered the trail public. 7. The opacity was a feature, not a bug. ProPublica's prior reporting — restated in the 26 June piece — is that 'SpaceX's approach was to let Chinese money in as long as it was routed through the Cayman Islands or other offshore secrecy hubs. The middleman structure handled the rest. An outside investor in a Tomales Bay fund does not show up on SpaceX's own cap table as a Chinese national. The opacity was not an accident. It was the product being sold.' This is a quoted conclusion from ProPublica's prior investigative reporting, not from SpaceX. The framing matters: a fund vehicle that does not show up on the cap table as foreign-domiciled is the product, and the product is sold to investors who specifically want exposure that is not visible on the company's books. 8. SpaceX has not denied the ledger. As of 26 June, SpaceX has not issued a public statement on the Kahlon ledger contents. The IPO is live. CFIUS review of public-defense-contractor IPOs is a documented process; the question is whether the ledger will be folded into that review. The silence is the asymmetric transparency signal: a court-unsealed record has been published by a Pulitzer-grade investigative outlet and the named company has not contested the record's contents. 9. The Pentagon contract-renewal timing. SpaceX has multiple major defense contracts (Falcon 9 / Falcon Heavy national-security launches, Starshield program, classified NRO constellation work) that are up for renewal or expansion in 2026-2027. The Kahlon ledger will be available to CFIUS, DoD, and the relevant oversight committees during those renewal reviews. The exposure is not retrospective — it is forward-looking, and the timing of the disclosure (one month after the IPO) is what makes it material. 10. The structural fingerprint. The structural fingerprint of this case — a public-defense-contractor cap table seeded with restricted-jurisdiction money through an insider-run fund middleman, then publicly excluded at IPO — is a recognizable pattern in defense-adjacent public offerings (Kaspersky lab equipment in USG networks; ByteDance/TikTok CFIUS case; the 2024 USG divestiture pressure on Chinese-linked investors in US semiconductor startups). The SpaceX case is distinctive in three ways: (a) the routing structure was an explicit fund product, not a single-investor thread; (b) the ledger is court-unsealed, not disclosed through regulatory action; (c) SpaceX has not denied the contents, which makes the asymmetry between posture and history admissible as a baseline for any subsequent review. 11. The Tomales Bay Capital defense. The structural defense available to SpaceX is that Tomales Bay Capital is a third-party fund manager whose investor composition is not SpaceX's responsibility — the cap table shows Tomales Bay as the investor, not the underlying LPs. This defense is the standard defense in fund-mediated foreign-investor cases and has succeeded in some regulatory contexts (most notably in the CFIUS review of certain pre-2018 Chinese investments in US semiconductors). It is unlikely to succeed as a complete defense for a public-defense-contractor cap table in 2026 because: (a) the CFIUS posture on public-defense-contractor IPOs has tightened since the 2023 outbound-investment rule; (b) the Pentagon has shown zero tolerance for ambiguity on foreign ownership in the post-TikTok environment; (c) the Delaware Supreme Court unsealing means the cap-table opacity argument is no longer available — the trail is now public. 12. The MPCi / David Su question. There is no allegation that Su or MPCi acted improperly. Both ProPublica and MPCi have stated there is no evidence of that. The structural point stands independently of any individual-investor conduct question: a Beijing-based venture firm was indirectly exposed to SpaceX during the period when SpaceX was winning its first major Pentagon launch contracts. The exposure was specifically engineered to be invisible on SpaceX's own cap table. The exposure is now public. The structural question is what happens next in the compliance review, not whether any individual acted badly.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: On 26 June 2026, ProPublica published an investigation revealing that SpaceX — which has publicly barred mainland-China and Hong-Kong investors from its June 2026 IPO — had already allowed at least a dozen investors with mainland-China, Hong-Kong, or Russia addresses into its cap table between 2018 and 2021, in checks ranging from $800,000 to $40 million. The routing ran through Tomales Bay Capital, an insider-run fund middleman (Iqbaljit Kahlon, whose tenure at SpaceX predates his own CFO's). The named anchor: a $15 million 2020 check from an entity tied to David Su, co-founder of the Beijing venture firm MPCi. The source: the Kahlon ledger, a sealed corporate-investor ledger that the Delaware Supreme Court ordered public this month in favor of ProPublica — the highest evidentiary tier available without an SEC investigation. SpaceX has not denied the ledger's contents. The compliance exposure ladder: CFIUS review, ITAR export rules, and Pentagon contract-eligibility standards all weight foreign ownership. Falcon 9 launches national-security payloads, Starshield is a dedicated defense product, Starship has DOD contracts — SpaceX sits at the center of the public-defense-contractor universe. The structural finding: the public exclusion posture (S-1 + post-IPO statements) and the historical inclusion practice (Kahlon ledger) are two different things, and the same defense-contractor compliance regime that the public posture was designed to satisfy now has a sealed-court-record basis to revisit. The opacity was the product. The product is now public.
